What are the 2 elements of agency (R3d § 1.01)?
column2: (1) P manifests assent that A will act on P's behalf and under P's control; (2) A consents.

column1: Is a contract or compensation required to form an agency?
column2: No. Only mutual consent to act on P's behalf and under P's control.

column1: Must the parties intend to create an "agency"?
column2: No. They need only consent to the relationship; the label doesn't matter.

column1: Why is agency an unstable form for running a business?
column2: It is terminable at will by either party.

column1: Gorton v. Doty: what created the agency?
column2: Lending the car on the condition that only the coach drive it supplied consent and control.

column1: Which case held that lending a car on condition only the borrower drive it made him the owner's agent?
column2: Gorton v. Doty.

column1: Cargill: when does a creditor become liable as a principal?
column2: When it takes de facto control over the debtor's business.

column1: Which case made a lender liable as principal for its debtor's debts because it controlled the business?
column2: A. Gay Jenson Farms v. Cargill.

column1: Cargill: did any single factor make Cargill the principal?
column2: No. The many control factors compounded (vetoes, audits, "paternal guidance," financing everything).

column1: How can a creditor avoid Cargill liability?
column2: Use ex ante loan covenants, give advice only, and rely on ex post creditor remedies.

column1: Name 4 of the Cargill control factors.
column2: Any 4: constant recommendations; right of first refusal; veto over mortgages/dividends; audits; criticizing finances; Cargill forms; financing everything; power to cut off financing.

column1: What are the 5 ways P can be bound to a contract A made?
column2: Actual authority (express or implied), apparent authority, inherent authority, ratification, estoppel.

column1: Actual authority is based on P's communications to whom?
column2: To the agent.

column1: Apparent authority is based on P's manifestations to whom?
column2: To the third party.

column1: R3d § 2.02: actual authority is measured from whose understanding?
column2: The agent's reasonable understanding of P's manifestations and objectives.

column1: What is implied actual authority?
column2: Authority to take steps necessary or incidental to an express instruction ("paint my house" → buy paint).

column1: When can custom create implied authority?
column2: When P grants broad discretion; not when P's instructions are detailed or A knows P doesn't know the custom.

column1: Is P bound by A's actually authorized act if T didn't know A was acting for anyone?
column2: Yes. Actual authority binds P regardless of T's knowledge.

column1: What are the 2 parts of the apparent authority test?
column2: (1) P held A out (or knowingly let A act) as authorized; (2) T reasonably and in good faith believed A was authorized.

column1: R3d § 3.03: can an agent create apparent authority by his own claims?
column2: No. It must be traceable to P's manifestation to T.

column1: When does apparent authority end?
column2: When T has notice that A's authority ended or P no longer consents.

column1: What counts as notice to T that apparent authority ended?
column2: P tells T directly, a reasonable time passes after a writing is delivered, or publicity reasonably likely to reach T.

column1: R3d § 6.01: with a disclosed principal, who are the parties to the contract?
column2: P and T. A is not a party unless A and T agree otherwise.

column1: Mill Street Church v. Hogan: what was the source of Bill's authority to hire his brother?
column2: Implied actual authority from past conduct: the church had let him hire Sam before.

column1: Which case found implied authority to hire a helper because the principal had allowed it on past jobs?
column2: Mill Street Church of Christ v. Hogan.

column1: Ackerman v. Sobol: does retaining a lawyer give the lawyer authority to settle?
column2: No, not by itself. But the client's course of dealing can create apparent authority.

column1: Ackerman v. Sobol: why was the client bound by the settlement?
column2: She took part in long settlement talks without objecting, creating apparent authority.

column1: R2d § 8A: what is inherent agency power?
column2: Power arising solely from the agency relationship, to protect third parties; not from authority or estoppel.

column1: What replaced inherent agency power in R3d?
column2: Broader apparent authority plus estoppel of an undisclosed principal (§ 2.06).

column1: Why does inherent authority put the loss on P?
column2: P is best placed to monitor A and avoid the loss.

column1: Watteau v. Fenwick: what is the rule?
column2: An undisclosed principal is liable for the agent's acts usual for that business, even acts P forbade.

column1: Watteau v. Fenwick: under what theory were the pub owners liable?
column2: Inherent agency power. There was no actual or apparent authority.

column1: Which case held secret pub owners liable for cigars their manager bought against orders?
column2: Watteau v. Fenwick.

column1: R3d § 2.06(2): can an undisclosed principal rely on secret limits on A's authority?
column2: No, not to cut A's authority below what T would assume if P were disclosed.

column1: What is ratification (R3d § 4.01)?
column2: P's after-the-fact affirmance of an act, treated as if done with actual authority.

column1: What 2 things must be true of P's ratification?
column2: P must be fully informed and must adopt the entire transaction.

column1: What are the 4 ways P can ratify?
column2: Expressly; by accepting benefits; by silence; by suing on the contract.

column1: R3d § 4.02(2): name the 3 situations where ratification is not effective.
column2: (a) Induced by fraud/misrepresentation; (b) in A's favor when P ratifies to avoid a loss; (c) to cut off third parties' prior rights.

column1: What are the 3 elements of agency by estoppel?
column2: (1) P creates an appearance of authority by words, acts, or omissions; (2) T reasonably relies in good faith; (3) T changes position.

column1: How does estoppel differ from apparent authority?
column2: It can arise from P's inaction or negligence, and T's belief need not be traceable to P's manifestation.

column1: Is estoppel a two-way street?
column2: No. P is estopped from denying authority, but T is not bound.

column1: Hoddeson v. Koos Bros.: why was the store liable to the customer who paid an imposter?
column2: Estoppel: the store failed to take reasonable steps to stop imposters on its sales floor.

column1: Which case held a store liable when a fake salesman took a customer's cash on its floor?
column2: Hoddeson v. Koos Bros.

column1: R3d § 1.04: define an undisclosed principal.
column2: T has no notice that A is acting for a principal.

column1: R3d § 1.04: define an unidentified principal.
column2: T knows A acts for a principal but not who it is.

column1: When is the agent personally liable on a contract?
column2: When the principal is undisclosed or unidentified.

column1: What 2 things must A disclose to avoid personal liability on a contract?
column2: (1) That A acts in a representative capacity; (2) P's identity.

column1: Does T have a duty to ask who the principal is?
column2: No.

column1: Atlantic Salmon v. Curran: why was Curran personally liable?
column2: He never disclosed his principal's identity, so the principal was unidentified.

column1: Which case held an agent personally liable for salmon bought for corporations he never identified?
column2: Atlantic Salmon A/S v. Curran.

column1: What are the 3 components of agency costs?
column2: Monitoring (by P), bonding (by A), and residual loss.

column1: What 2 jobs do fiduciary duties do in agency?
column2: Fill gaps in incomplete contracts and act as an ex post bond making A's promises credible.

column1: What are the 3 fiduciary duties of an agent?
column2: Obedience, care, loyalty.

column1: Which R3d section is the duty of obedience?
column2: § 8.09 (act within actual authority, follow instructions).

column1: What are the 3 classic breaches of an agent's duty of loyalty?
column2: (1) Bribe or kickback from T; (2) secret profit dealing with P; (3) using the position to profit from someone unrelated to P.

column1: R2d § 389: may A deal with P as an adverse party?
column2: Not without P's knowledge (e.g., an agent hired to sell can't secretly buy).

column1: R3d § 8.04: may an agent prepare to compete during the agency?
column2: Yes, if not otherwise wrongful. Actually competing during the agency is barred.

column1: R3d § 8.05: what makes departure preparations wrongful?
column2: Using P's property or confidential information.

column1: Reading v. Regem: what is the rule?
column2: An agent who uses his position to make a profit must account for it to P, even if P lost nothing.

column1: Reading v. Regem: why did the Crown get the sergeant's money?
column2: He earned it by using his position (the uniform), not his own efforts.

column1: Which case made a soldier hand over bribes earned escorting smugglers in uniform?
column2: Reading v. Regem.

column1: Reading hypos: what is the test for whether P gets A's profit?
column2: Did the money come from the agency position or from something A did on his own?

column1: Reading hypo: may a war hero keep money a restaurant pays him to show up?
column2: Yes. He is cashing in on honestly earned fame, not misusing a position.

column1: Rash v. J.V. Intermediate: what did Rash fail to do?
column2: Disclose that he owned the scaffolding company he steered subcontracts to.

column1: Rash v. J.V. Intermediate: how is the scope of the duty to disclose judged?
column2: For the specific transaction: what P should rightly know.

column1: Town & Country v. Newbery: what may former employees not do, even without a non-compete?
column2: Solicit customers from a list the employer built at significant effort and expense.

column1: Town & Country v. Newbery: why was the customer list protected?
column2: It was built by cold-calling and screening, so it was a confidential asset.

column1: Which case held employees can't solicit customers from a list the employer built at great effort?
column2: Town & Country House & Home Service v. Newbery.

column1: Which case held a manager breached by not disclosing his stake in a subcontractor?
column2: Rash v. J.V. Intermediate.

column1: Which case bound a client to a settlement after she sat through her lawyer's negotiations?
column2: Ackerman v. Sobol Family Partnership.

column1: UPA § 6(1): define a partnership.
column2: An association of two or more persons to carry on as co-owners a business for profit.

column1: Can a partnership form without the parties intending one?
column2: Yes. It is the default form for co-owners of a for-profit business.

column1: What are the 3 elements of a partnership?
column2: (1) Intent to be partners; (2) co-ownership of the business; (3) profit motive.

column1: Which partnership element usually decides close cases?
column2: Co-ownership.

column1: Under UPA § 7 / RUPA § 202, what does sharing profits create?
column2: A presumption (prima facie evidence) of partnership.

column1: When does sharing profits NOT create a presumption of partnership?
column2: When received as debt payments, wages, rent, or an annuity.

column1: Does co-owning property by itself create a partnership?
column2: No, even if the co-owners share profits from it.

column1: Name 4 Fenwick factors for whether a partnership exists.
column2: Any 4: intent; profit sharing; loss sharing; control of property; shared administration; agreement's language; conduct toward third parties; rights on dissolution.

column1: Fenwick: why was the "partner" receptionist really an employee?
column2: No co-ownership: no capital, no control, no share of losses.

column1: Which case held that calling a receptionist a "partner" with 20% of profits didn't make her one?
column2: Fenwick v. Unemployment Compensation Commission.

column1: Martin v. Peyton: what is the rule?
column2: A lender is a partner only if it carries on the business as a co-owner.

column1: Martin v. Peyton: did inspection rights, a veto, and 40% of profits make the lenders partners?
column2: No. They were protections for a loan, not control.

column1: Southex v. RIBA: is calling someone a "partner" in the agreement dispositive?
column2: No. Labels are probative but not dispositive; look at the totality.

column1: Southex: why was there no partnership despite a 55/45 profit split?
column2: SEM bore all losses and contracted with third parties in its own name.

column1: Young v. Jones: what does partnership by estoppel require?
column2: That the third party actually relied on the representation of partnership.

column1: Which case rejected partnership by estoppel because investors never saw the "global partnership" brochure?
column2: Young v. Jones.

column1: Which 2 duties does UPA § 409 impose on partners?
column2: Loyalty and care.

column1: Why do partners owe no duty of obedience?
column2: They are co-owners with no principal to obey.

column1: § 409(b)(1): what must a partner account for?
column2: Any benefit from the business, from using partnership property, or from taking a partnership opportunity.

column1: Which subsection of § 409 codifies Meinhard?
column2: § 409(b)(1)(C): appropriation of a partnership opportunity.

column1: § 409(b)(3): when is a partner barred from competing with the partnership?
column2: Before dissolution.

column1: § 409(c): what is the partner's standard of care?
column2: Refrain from gross negligence, recklessness, intentional misconduct, or knowing violation of law.

column1: Does ordinary negligence breach a partner's duty of care?
column2: No. § 409(c) requires gross negligence or worse.

column1: § 105(d): how can partners authorize a deal that would breach loyalty?
column2: Approval by disinterested, independent persons after full disclosure, per a method in the agreement.

column1: Meinhard v. Salmon: what standard of loyalty do joint adventurers owe?
column2: "Not honesty alone, but the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive."

column1: Meinhard v. Salmon: what did Salmon have to do with the new lease opportunity?
column2: Disclose it to Meinhard, because it came to him through the venture.

column1: Meinhard v. Salmon: what was the remedy?
column2: A constructive trust for Meinhard.

column1: Meinhard: what was the dissent's argument?
column2: The venture had a fixed end and limited purpose, so the new lease was outside it.

column1: What is the economic case for the Meinhard disclosure rule?
column2: Without it, partners would hoard information and squeeze each other out; a default rule is cheaper than contracting.

column1: Sandvick v. LaCrosse: do joint venturers owe fiduciary duties without a partnership?
column2: Yes, within the scope of the venture.

column1: Which case held co-investors breached loyalty by secretly buying "top leases" on venture land?
column2: Sandvick v. LaCrosse.

column1: What is the 3-step Sandvick framework?
column2: (1) Partnership? (2) If not, joint venture? (3) What is the scope of the venture, and what duties follow?

column1: What are the 4 elements of a joint venture?
column2: (1) Contribution; (2) proprietary interest and mutual control; (3) agreement to share profits; (4) contract (express or implied).

column1: Graubard: what may departing partners tell clients, and when?
column2: After telling the firm: that they are leaving and that the client may choose counsel.

column1: Graubard: name 3 things departing partners may not do.
column2: Secretly lure clients; mislead clients about their choice; lie to partners about leaving (or leave abruptly with clients and files).

column1: Meehan v. Shaughnessy: is preparing to leave a breach?
column2: No. Lying about leaving and unfair client solicitation are.

column1: Meehan v. Shaughnessy: what 2 things were breaches?
column2: Denying they were leaving when asked, and sending clients one-sided letters.

column1: RUPA § 601(4): how can partners expel a partner without a court?
column2: Unanimous vote of the others, plus one of 4 listed conditions.

column1: RUPA § 601(5): name the 3 grounds for judicial expulsion.
column2: (1) Wrongful conduct materially harming the business; (2) willful or persistent material breach; (3) conduct making it impracticable to continue with the partner.

column1: Lawlis v. Kightlinger & Gray: can a partner be expelled without cause?
column2: Yes, under a "guillotine" clause in the agreement.

column1: Lawlis: when would expulsion breach a fiduciary duty?
column2: Only if money owed to the expelled partner were wrongfully withheld.

column1: What does Lawlis say about the nature of partner fiduciary duties?
column2: They work like default rules the agreement can pare back.

column1: Partnership finance: what is a draw?
column2: A periodic distribution of profits.

column1: Partnership finance: what is an advance?
column2: A partner's loan to the firm, repaid with interest.

column1: By default, are partners paid a salary for their services?
column2: No. They get distributions only, unless they agree otherwise.

column1: RUPA § 204: what 3 things do you check to see if property belongs to the partnership?
column2: Title, then capacity (acting as partner), then whose money paid for it.

column1: RUPA § 204(3): what presumption arises if partnership funds bought the property?
column2: It is presumed partnership property.

column1: RUPA § 401(a): what is the default split of profits?
column2: Equal shares.

column1: RUPA § 401(a): what is the default split of losses?
column2: In proportion to each partner's share of profits.

column1: UPA (1914) § 40(b): what is the 4-tier order of payment on winding up?
column2: Outside creditors → partner loans → capital → profits.

column1: RUPA § 806: what is the 3-tier order of payment on winding up?
column2: Creditors (including partner-lenders) → capital → profits.

column1: How did the 1997 act collapse 4 tiers into 3?
column2: It put partners who lent money in the same class as outside creditors.

column1: In re Fulton: what determines whether property belongs to the partnership?
column2: The partners' intent at acquisition.

column1: In re Fulton: what does a partner's bankruptcy estate get?
column2: Only his partnership interest, not partnership property.

column1: Fulton hypo: trailer sells for $4K, creditor owed $1K, Carroll contributed $4K. Who gets what?
column2: Creditor $1K, Carroll $3K, Fulton $0.

column1: What is the "sweat equity" problem in returning capital first, and the fix?
column2: The labor partner gets nothing for work; fix with market salary plus market interest on capital.

column1: RUPA § 301(1): when does a partner's ordinary-course act bind the firm?
column2: Always, unless the partner lacked authority AND T knew or had notice of that.

column1: RUPA § 401(k): what vote is needed for an ordinary-course matter?
column2: A majority of partners.

column1: RUPA § 401(k): what vote is needed for an extraordinary act or amendment?
column2: Unanimous consent.

column1: What did the 1997 act change in § 301(1)?
column2: The firm escapes if T "knew or had notice" of no authority (1914 required actual knowledge).

column1: National Biscuit v. Stroud: can one of two equal partners cut off the other's authority?
column2: No. Restricting a partner's authority takes a majority.

column1: Which case bound a 2-person partnership to a bread order one partner had told the seller he wouldn't pay for?
column2: National Biscuit Co. v. Stroud.

column1: Summers v. Dooley: can one of two equal partners impose a new expense over the other's objection?
column2: No. No majority approved it.

column1: Which case denied a partner reimbursement for hiring a third worker his equal partner refused?
column2: Summers v. Dooley.

column1: How do Stroud and Summers fit together?
column2: Same majority rule: the partner trying to change the status quo without a majority loses.

column1: Day v. Sidley & Austin: may partners delegate management to an executive committee?
column2: Yes.

column1: Day v. Sidley & Austin: what's needed for a fiduciary breach?
column2: Self-dealing, profit, or loss to the firm, not just nondisclosure of structural changes.

column1: Dissociation vs. dissolution?
column2: Dissociation: a partner leaves. Dissolution: the business ends and winds up.

column1: Does dissociation always cause dissolution?
column2: No.

column1: At-will vs. term partnership?
column2: At-will: any partner can dissolve anytime. Term: has a set term or undertaking.

column1: Name 3 events that are NOT dissociation by default.
column2: Any 3: transferring an interest; a charging order; adding a partner; disagreements.

column1: RUPA § 601: name 4 events that cause dissociation.
column2: Any 4: notice of withdrawal; agreed event; expulsion; bankruptcy; death or incapacity.

column1: RUPA § 701: at what value is a dissociated partner bought out?
column2: The greater of liquidation value or going-concern value, minus damages for wrongful dissociation.

column1: RUPA § 801: in an at-will partnership, what does a partner's withdrawal trigger?
column2: Dissolution and winding up.

column1: RUPA § 801: how can a term partnership dissolve early after a partner's death or wrongful dissociation?
column2: If at least half the remaining partners vote to wind up within 90 days.

column1: RUPA § 802: after dissolution, does a partner have actual authority for new business?
column2: No. Only authority to wind up.

column1: How do partners end lingering apparent authority after dissolution?
column2: File a § 704 statement; T is deemed on notice 90 days later.

column1: Giles v. Giles Land Co.: when can a court dissociate a partner?
column2: When his wrongful conduct materially harms the business or makes continuing with him impracticable.

column1: Which case judicially dissociated a son whose hostility brought the family farm business to a standstill?
column2: Giles v. Giles Land Co.

column1: Brennan v. Brennan Associates: why could the court order dissociation?
column2: An irreparable breakdown justifies dissolution, so it also justifies the lesser remedy of dissociation.

column1: Kovacik v. Reed: must a labor-only partner share a capital partner's losses?
column2: No. Each loses what he put in.

column1: How does Kovacik relate to RUPA § 401(a)?
column2: It's a judicial gloss; read literally, § 401(a) would make losses follow the profit share.

column1: G&S Investments v. Belman: does filing a dissolution suit dissolve the partnership?
column2: No.

column1: G&S Investments: what does "capital account" mean in a buy-out clause?
column2: The book figure, not market value.

column1: RUPA § 306(a): how are general partners liable for partnership obligations?
column2: Jointly and severally, for everything.

column1: UPA (1914) § 15: how were partners liable?
column2: Jointly and severally for torts; only jointly for other debts.

column1: LLP: who gets limited liability?
column2: All partners, once the general partnership registers.

column1: LP: who manages and who is personally liable?
column2: Only the general partners.

column1: LLC: what 2 things does it combine?
column2: Partnership (pass-through) taxation and corporate limited liability.

column1: Frigidaire v. Union Properties: did LPs who ran the corporate GP lose limited liability?
column2: No. They controlled the business only as officers and directors of the corporate GP.

column1: Which case held a dissolution suit doesn't dissolve the firm and "capital account" means book value?
column2: G&S Investments v. Belman.

column1: Which case kept LPs' limited liability though they ran the corporate GP?
column2: Frigidaire Sales v. Union Properties.

column1: Which case held a capital-only partner can't make a labor-only partner share capital losses?
column2: Kovacik v. Reed.

column1: Which case upheld expelling a partner without cause under a guillotine clause?
column2: Lawlis v. Kightlinger & Gray.

column1: Which case held departing partners breached by lying about leaving and sending one-sided client letters?
column2: Meehan v. Shaughnessy.

column1: Which case held lenders with a veto and 40% of profits were not partners?
column2: Martin v. Peyton.

column1: Which case required a joint adventurer to share a lease renewal he took secretly?
column2: Meinhard v. Salmon.

column1: Which case held a trailer was partnership property, out of a bankrupt partner's estate?
column2: In re Fulton.

column1: Which case allowed delegating firm management to an executive committee without breach?
column2: Day v. Sidley & Austin.

column1: What are the 5 critical attributes of a corporation?
column2: Legal personality; limited liability; separation of ownership and control; liquidity; flexible capital structure.

column1: Can an individual director bind the corporation?
column2: No. Directors aren't agents; the board acts as a body.

column1: MBCA § 8.01(b) / DGCL § 141(a): who manages the corporation?
column2: The board, or others under its direction.

column1: Name the 4 things shareholders vote on.
column2: Directors; charter and bylaw amendments; mergers; odds and ends (e.g., auditors).

column1: MBCA § 6.22(b): what are the 2 exceptions to SH limited liability?
column2: (1) The articles provide otherwise; (2) the SH's own acts or conduct.

column1: What are the 3 steps to amend the articles?
column2: Board recommends → SHs approve → file with the state.

column1: If the bylaws conflict with the articles, which wins?
column2: The articles.

column1: What is the internal affairs doctrine?
column2: Only the state of incorporation governs relations among the corporation, its D&Os, and SHs.

column1: DGCL § 109(a): who holds the power to amend bylaws by default?
column2: The shareholders.

column1: DGCL § 109(a): if the charter gives the board bylaw power, do SHs lose it?
column2: No. Both hold it.

column1: DGCL § 109(b): what may bylaws contain?
column2: Anything about the business, its affairs, or constituents' rights, if consistent with law and the charter.

column1: Boilermakers v. Chevron: can a board adopt a forum-selection bylaw without a SH vote?
column2: Yes, if the charter gives it bylaw power.

column1: Boilermakers v. Chevron: why was the forum bylaw valid?
column2: It regulates where, not whether, SHs sue, and SHs bought knowing the board could amend bylaws.

column1: VantagePoint v. Examen: which state's law governed the class vote on the merger?
column2: Delaware (state of incorporation), not California.

column1: Affirmative asset partitioning means...
column2: SHs' personal creditors can't reach the firm's assets.

column1: Defensive asset partitioning means...
column2: The firm's creditors can't reach SHs' personal assets (limited liability).

column1: What are the 2 main downsides of limited liability?
column2: Externalities on third parties and excessive risk-taking.

column1: What are the 3 theories for reaching past the corporation (Walkovszky)?
column2: Enterprise liability, agency, veil piercing.

column1: Enterprise liability lets the plaintiff recover from whom?
column2: Sister corporations treated as one, not the shareholders.

column1: Which of the 3 Walkovszky theories is weakest?
column2: Agency.

column1: Walkovszky v. Carlton: is undercapitalization with minimum insurance enough to pierce?
column2: No.

column1: Walkovszky: what must P show to hold the SH personally liable?
column2: That he used the corporation to conduct his own personal business.

column1: Walkovszky: what did the dissent argue?
column2: Deliberately undercapitalized public-service corps should expose their SHs.

column1: Sea-Land v. Pepper Source: what are the 2 prongs for piercing?
column2: (1) Unity of interest so no separate personalities exist; (2) respecting the form would sanction fraud or promote injustice.

column1: Sea-Land: is an unpaid debt enough injustice to pierce?
column2: No. Every piercing case involves one.

column1: Name the 4 Sea-Land unity-of-interest factors.
column2: No corporate formalities; commingling; undercapitalization; one corp using another's assets.

column1: Sea-Land: what satisfied the injustice prong on remand?
column2: Proof of tax fraud.

column1: Which case refused to pierce a taxi fleet split into two-cab corporations?
column2: Walkovszky v. Carlton.

column1: Which case set the 2-prong unity-of-interest + injustice test for piercing?
column2: Sea-Land Services v. Pepper Source.

column1: Which case upheld a board-adopted forum-selection bylaw?
column2: Boilermakers Local 154 v. Chevron.

column1: Which case applied Delaware law to a DE corp's class vote despite California's statute?
column2: VantagePoint Venture Partners v. Examen.

column1: What was Friedman's view of corporate social responsibility?
column2: The only one is to increase profits within the rules of the game.

column1: What are the 3 recurring contexts for corporate-purpose disputes?
column2: Charitable giving; forced dividends; a controller indulging private whims.

column1: DGCL § 122(9): may a corporation make charitable donations?
column2: Yes. It is an express corporate power.

column1: Does § 122(9) grant a power or a purpose?
column2: A power.

column1: A.P. Smith v. Barlow: when may a corporation make a charitable gift?
column2: When it is reasonable and reasonably believed to advance the public interest and the corporation's own.

column1: A.P. Smith: why was the gift to Princeton valid?
column2: It was modest, within statutory limits, and aimed at goodwill and a trained workforce.

column1: A.P. Smith: does a later-enacted donation statute apply to existing corporations?
column2: Yes.

column1: DGCL § 170(a): what are the 2 sources for dividends?
column2: Surplus, or if none, net profits for the current and/or prior fiscal year.

column1: What are "nimble dividends"?
column2: Dividends paid from current or prior-year net profits when there is no surplus.

column1: DGCL § 174(a): who is liable for an unlawful dividend, and for how long?
column2: Directors, jointly and severally, for 6 years.

column1: DGCL § 172: what protects a director who approved a dividend?
column2: Good-faith reliance on officers, counsel, or accountants.

column1: MBCA § 6.40: what are the 2 tests for any distribution?
column2: Equity insolvency (can pay debts as due) and balance sheet (assets exceed liabilities + preferences).

column1: Dodge v. Ford: for whose benefit is a corporation primarily run?
column2: The shareholders' profit.

column1: Dodge v. Ford: what did the court order and what did it refuse?
column2: Ordered dividends; refused to enjoin the River Rouge expansion.

column1: Of Dodge, Kamin, and Shlensky, which granted relief?
column2: Dodge v. Ford.

column1: Shlensky v. Wrigley: what 3 things would let a court review a business decision?
column2: Fraud, illegality, or conflict of interest.

column1: Which case refused to make the Cubs install lights for night games?
column2: Shlensky v. Wrigley.

column1: Which case held an informed board's choice to forgo a tax loss was protected by the BJR?
column2: Kamin v. American Express.

column1: Which case upheld a charitable gift to Princeton?
column2: A.P. Smith Mfg. Co. v. Barlow.

column1: Which case ordered Ford to pay dividends?
column2: Dodge v. Ford Motor Co.

column1: What does the BJR presume directors did?
column2: Acted on an informed basis, in good faith, and in the honest belief it served the corporation.

column1: What does even a BJR-protected decision need?
column2: A rational business purpose.

column1: What standard of negligence breaches the duty of care in practice?
column2: Gross negligence.

column1: If P rebuts the BJR, what must directors prove?
column2: Entire fairness: fair dealing and fair price.

column1: Cede v. Technicolor: what is the "triad" P can breach to rebut the BJR?
column2: Good faith, loyalty, due care.

column1: Does losing the BJR mean the directors lose the case?
column2: No. They can still prove entire fairness.

column1: Kamin v. American Express: is a poor decision by an informed board actionable?
column2: No. Mere errors of judgment aren't; need fraud, bad faith, or self-dealing.

column1: Kamin: why was the claim dismissed?
column2: The board knew the tax consequences and chose anyway: an informed decision.

column1: Smith v. Van Gorkom: what is the rule?
column2: The BJR doesn't protect an uninformed decision; failing to get reasonably available information is gross negligence.

column1: Van Gorkom: why didn't § 141(e) reliance protect the board?
column2: There was no real report to rely on, just a 20-minute oral presentation.

column1: Van Gorkom: why didn't the SH vote cure the problem?
column2: The shareholders weren't fully informed.

column1: Which case held a board grossly negligent for approving a $55/share sale after a 20-minute presentation with no valuation?
column2: Smith v. Van Gorkom.

column1: Van Gorkom process roadmap: name 4 things a board should do.
column2: Any 4: consult management and outside advisors; get a valuation; negotiate at arm's length; resist time pressure; get informed.

column1: DGCL § 141(e): when are directors protected in relying on reports?
column2: When relying in good faith on officers, committees, or experts reasonably selected and believed competent.

column1: DGCL § 251(b): what must the board do before sending a merger to SHs?
column2: Approve it and declare it advisable: make its own informed judgment.

column1: What did Delaware enact in response to Van Gorkom?
column2: DGCL § 102(b)(7) exculpation.

column1: § 102(b)(7): what can the charter eliminate?
column2: Personal money damages for D&O breaches of the duty of care.

column1: § 102(b)(7): name the 4 things the charter can never exculpate.
column2: Loyalty breaches; bad faith or knowing violations; § 174 unlawful dividends; improper personal benefit.

column1: Does § 102(b)(7) eliminate injunctive relief for care breaches?
column2: No. Only money damages.

column1: Francis v. United Jersey Bank: is ignorance or incapacity a defense for a passive director?
column2: No. An incapable director should resign.

column1: Which case held a director liable for never attending meetings while her sons looted the company?
column2: Francis v. United Jersey Bank.

column1: Can a decision not to act get the BJR?
column2: Yes, if it was informed. Simply doing nothing isn't a business judgment.

column1: Why is loyalty never exculpable but care is?
column2: Loyalty breaches are deliberate (stealing); care breaches are shirking.

column1: What happens to the BJR when a director has a conflict?
column2: It is lost and the burden shifts to the director to prove fairness.

column1: DGCL § 144(a): name the 3 safe-harbor routes for an interested transaction.
column2: (1) Informed disinterested-director approval; (2) informed disinterested-SH approval; (3) fairness.

column1: How many § 144(a) routes must be satisfied?
column2: Any one.

column1: SB 21 § 144(a)(1): what standard must the approving directors meet?
column2: Good faith and without gross negligence.

column1: SB 21 § 144(a)(1): what if most of the board is conflicted?
column2: A committee of 2+ disinterested directors must approve.

column1: Where did SB 21 move controlling-SH transactions?
column2: New DGCL § 144(b) and (c).

column1: Bayer v. Beran: how did the directors win despite the conflict?
column2: They proved the transaction was fair.

column1: Which case upheld a company hiring the president's wife to sing in its radio ads because the pay was fair?
column2: Bayer v. Beran.

column1: Benihana: what satisfies § 144(a)(1) for a director's conflict?
column2: Disinterested directors knowing the material facts of it.

column1: Benihana: did diluting the controlling holder defeat the BJR?
column2: No. There was a real need for capital; dilution was a side effect.

column1: Related-party transaction vs. corporate opportunity?
column2: Related: insider deals with the corporation. Opportunity: insider takes a third-party deal belonging to the corporation.

column1: Who is bound by the corporate opportunity doctrine?
column2: Officers, directors, and dominant SHs active in management.

column1: What are the 4 Broz factors?
column2: (1) Corp financially able; (2) in its line of business; (3) corp has an interest or expectancy; (4) taking it creates a conflict.

column1: Broz: must an insider formally present an opportunity to the board?
column2: No.

column1: Broz: why was there no breach?
column2: CIS couldn't afford the license and its CEO and a director said they weren't interested.

column1: How should you apply Broz on the exam?
column2: Run all 4 factors and name the gating one.

column1: In re eBay: what were the IPO allocations to executives?
column2: A corporate opportunity (effectively kickbacks for eBay's banking business).

column1: In re eBay: how broadly was "line of business" read?
column2: Broadly enough to cover investing cash in securities.

column1: What makes a SH a "controller"?
column2: Majority ownership, or a minority stake with actual control of the board or the transaction.

column1: When does a controller deal get entire fairness instead of BJR?
column2: When it's self-dealing: the controller takes a benefit to the exclusion and detriment of the minority.

column1: What are the 2 MFW conditions for BJR on a controller deal?
column2: (1) Independent special committee with power to say no; (2) informed majority-of-the-minority vote.

column1: MFW: what happens if only one of the 2 conditions is met?
column2: Burden shifts to P, but review stays entire fairness.

column1: Fliegler v. Lawrence: what ratification shifts the burden?
column2: Approval by a majority of disinterested SHs.

column1: Fliegler: why didn't the SH vote shift the burden?
column2: Interested SHs carried the vote.

column1: Investors Bancorp: does approving a general equity plan ratify specific director awards?
column2: No. SHs must approve the specific awards.

column1: DGCL § 123 authorizes what structure?
column2: Parent–subsidiary: a corporation may own and vote other corporations' securities.

column1: Which case held a CIS director could take a cellular license CIS couldn't afford and didn't want?
column2: Broz v. Cellular Information Systems.

column1: Which case held SH approval of a broad equity plan didn't ratify directors' later self-awards?
column2: In re Investors Bancorp.

column1: Which case held ratification by interested SHs doesn't shift the burden?
column2: Fliegler v. Lawrence.

column1: Which case held IPO shares given to executives for the company's banking business were a corporate opportunity?
column2: In re eBay Shareholders Litigation.

column1: Which case upheld a dilutive preferred-stock deal negotiated by a conflicted director the board knew about?
column2: Benihana of Tokyo v. Benihana.

column1: Name the 3 DGCL protections that bad faith defeats.
column2: § 141(e) reliance, § 102(b)(7) exculpation, § 145 indemnification.

column1: DGCL § 145: what is required for indemnification?
column2: Good faith and reasonable belief the conduct was in or not opposed to the corporation's interests.

column1: Can advancement of legal fees be owed before the merits are decided?
column2: Yes (Frank/Javice), even though indemnification requires good faith.

column1: Disney: what are the 2 kinds of conduct that ARE bad faith?
column2: Subjective intent to harm, and intentional dereliction (conscious disregard) of duty.

column1: Disney: is gross negligence alone bad faith?
column2: No. It's a care problem, exculpable under § 102(b)(7).

column1: Disney: does falling short of best practices lose the BJR?
column2: No, if directors were reasonably informed and had a rational business purpose.

column1: Disney: why wasn't Ovitz's package waste?
column2: It had a rational purpose: it was needed to lure him from CAA.

column1: What is "say on pay"?
column2: Dodd-Frank's advisory SH vote on executive pay, at least every 3 years.

column1: What standard applies to executive compensation by default?
column2: Intrinsic fairness, because pay is inherently conflicted.

column1: Graham (1963): must directors install a monitoring system absent suspicion?
column2: No. No "corporate system of espionage"; they must respond to red flags.

column1: Caremark: what must directors attempt in good faith?
column2: To ensure an adequate information and reporting system exists.

column1: Caremark: what level of failure creates oversight liability?
column2: A sustained or systematic failure (an utter failure to try).

column1: Caremark: was the oversight duty a holding?
column2: No. It was dicta; the court approved a settlement.

column1: Why doesn't the BJR fit oversight cases?
column2: There is no board decision to defer to.

column1: Stone v. Ritter: what are the 2 ways to prove oversight liability?
column2: (1) Utter failure to implement any reporting system; (2) conscious failure to monitor an existing one.

column1: Stone v. Ritter: which duty does an oversight failure breach?
column2: Loyalty, via bad faith.

column1: Stone v. Ritter: is good faith a third independent duty?
column2: No.

column1: Why does it matter that oversight failure is a loyalty breach?
column2: It can't be exculpated under § 102(b)(7) or indemnified under § 145.

column1: Stone v. Ritter: why was demand not excused?
column2: A KPMG report showed the board had a real compliance system and ignored no red flags.

column1: MBCA § 8.01(c): name 4 oversight areas for a public board.
column2: Any 4: performance; major risks; officer pay; compliance; financial statements; internal controls; information flow; board composition.

column1: Which case first said directors must try in good faith to ensure a reporting system exists?
column2: In re Caremark International Derivative Litigation.

column1: Which case adopted Caremark as Delaware law and placed oversight failure under loyalty?
column2: Stone v. Ritter.

column1: Which case held the Ovitz hiring and no-fault firing payout was not bad faith or waste?
column2: In re Walt Disney Co. Derivative Litigation.

column1: Direct suit vs. derivative suit?
column2: Direct: injury to the SH, recovery to the SH. Derivative: injury to the corporation, recovery to it.

column1: What are the 2 Tooley questions?
column2: (1) Who suffered the harm, the corporation or the SHs individually? (2) Who would get the recovery?

column1: Where does derivative recovery usually go?
column2: To the corporation.

column1: In re Medtronic: were the SHs' capital-gains taxes from the inversion direct or derivative?
column2: Direct.

column1: In re Medtronic: was reimbursing D&Os' excise taxes direct or derivative?
column2: Derivative (waste of corporate funds).

column1: Why do derivative suits tend to settle too cheaply?
column2: P's lawyer is the real party in interest, and Ds want to keep indemnification.

column1: FRCP 23.1: what must the complaint plead with particularity?
column2: Demand efforts, or why no demand was made.

column1: FRCP 23.1: what is needed to settle or dismiss a derivative suit?
column2: Court approval and notice to SHs.

column1: What does the demand requirement really decide?
column2: Who controls the litigation: the SH or the board.

column1: What happens if P makes demand in Delaware?
column2: P concedes demand was required; the board's refusal gets the BJR and P almost always loses.

column1: Aronson: what are the 2 prongs for demand futility?
column2: Reasonable doubt that (1) directors are disinterested and independent, or (2) the transaction was a valid business judgment.

column1: Aronson: is being named a defendant and voting for the deal enough to excuse demand?
column2: No.

column1: Rales: what does the test ask?
column2: Whether the board as of filing could impartially consider a demand.

column1: Name the 3 situations where Rales applied.
column2: Majority of board replaced; no board decision challenged (e.g., oversight); decision by a different corporation's board.

column1: Zuckerberg: what are the 3 questions asked director by director?
column2: (i) Material personal benefit? (ii) Substantial likelihood of liability? (iii) Lacks independence from someone who does?

column1: Zuckerberg: how many directors must fail the test to excuse demand?
column2: At least half of the demand board.

column1: Zuckerberg: do exculpated care claims create a substantial likelihood of liability?
column2: No.

column1: On the exam, which demand-futility test should you apply?
column2: Only the Zuckerberg test.

column1: Zuckerberg: were business ties, friendship, and gratitude enough to excuse demand?
column2: No.

column1: Even when demand is excused, how can the corporation still end the suit?
column2: A special litigation committee of independent directors can move to dismiss.

column1: Which DGCL section authorizes an SLC?
DGCL § 141(c)(2): name the 2 things a committee can't do.
column2: Approve matters requiring SH approval; amend bylaws.

column1: Zapata step 1: what must the corporation prove about the SLC?
column2: Independence, good faith, a reasonable investigation, and reasonable bases for its conclusions.

column1: Zapata step 2: what may the court do?
column2: Apply its own business judgment on whether to dismiss.

column1: Zapata: who bears the burden at step 1?
column2: The corporation.

column1: Auerbach v. Bennett (NY): what does the court review?
column2: Only the SLC's independence and the adequacy of its procedures; the decision gets the BJR.

column1: Zapata vs. Auerbach: which is more deferential to the SLC?
column2: Auerbach (NY).

column1: Disinterested vs. independent?
column2: Disinterested: no personal stake. Independent: no ties making the director beholden to an interested person.

column1: Sanchez: how must friendship and financial ties be analyzed?
column2: Together, not separately.

column1: Sanchez: why did director Jackson lack independence?
column2: Decades-long close friendship with the chair plus financial dependence on a Sanchez-affiliated job.

column1: Is moving in the same social circles enough to lose independence?
column2: No (Sanchez).

column1: Aronson: does a 47% holder who picked every director make the board non-independent?
column2: No. P must show the directors are beholden.

column1: SB 21: what presumption do exchange-independent directors get?
column2: A stronger, rebuttable presumption of disinterestedness.

column1: Which case set the 2-step test for a special litigation committee's motion to dismiss?
column2: Zapata Corp. v. Maldonado.

column1: Which case sets the universal demand-futility test?
column2: United Food & Commercial Workers Union v. Zuckerberg.

column1: Which case split a tax-inversion suit into direct and derivative claims?
column2: In re Medtronic Shareholder Litigation.

column1: Which case held friendship plus financial ties together can defeat a director's independence?
column2: Delaware County Employees Retirement Fund v. Sanchez.

column1: Which act governs the primary market and which the secondary?
column2: '33 Act: primary (issuer sales). '34 Act: secondary (trading).

column1: Does the SEC review an offering's investment merit?
column2: No. Only disclosure.

column1: How are courts' tests for a "security" oriented?
column2: Economic substance over form or label.

column1: What are the 4 Howey prongs?
column2: (i) Investment of money; (ii) common enterprise; (iii) reasonable expectation of profits; (iv) from the efforts of others.

column1: Howey prong (iv): what's the key question?
column2: Is the investor unable to exercise meaningful control?

column1: Robinson v. Glynn: why wasn't the LLC interest an investment contract?
column2: Robinson had meaningful control as treasurer and vice-chair.

column1: Robinson v. Glynn: why wasn't the LLC interest "stock"?
column2: It lacked the name and usual traits of stock (not freely negotiable, no shares).

column1: Securities Act § 5: name the 3 rules.
column2: No offers before filing; no sales before effectiveness; deliver a prospectus before sale.

column1: Exempt security vs. exempt transaction?
column2: Exempt security never needs registration; exempt transaction is one-time, so resale needs its own exemption.

column1: What are the 6 elements of a 10b-5 claim?
column2: Material misstatement/omission; scienter; connection to a purchase or sale; reliance; economic loss; loss causation.

column1: Is negligence enough for 10b-5 scienter?
column2: No. Intent, and usually recklessness, is required.

column1: When is a fact "material"?
column2: A reasonable investor would likely consider it important.

column1: What did Basic v. Levinson create?
column2: A rebuttable presumption of reliance (fraud on the market).

column1: Which form of the ECMH underlies Basic?
column2: Semi-strong: prices reflect all public information.

column1: Halliburton: did the Court overrule Basic?
column2: No.

column1: Halliburton: what can defendants do at class certification?
column2: Rebut the presumption with evidence of no price impact.

column1: West v. Prudential: why no fraud-on-the-market presumption?
column2: The lies were private, so they couldn't affect the market price.

column1: West v. Prudential: which form of the ECMH did it reject?
column2: Strong form.

column1: What are the 4 elements of insider trading?
column2: Breach of duty; trading on MNPI; scienter; (for tips) personal benefit.

column1: Classical theory: who owes the duty, and to whom?
column2: Insiders and temporary insiders, to the issuer's SHs.

column1: Misappropriation theory: to whom is the duty owed?
column2: To the source of the information.

column1: Who are "temporary insiders"?
column2: Outside professionals such as lawyers, accountants, underwriters, consultants.

column1: Rule 10b5-1: what does trading "on the basis of" MNPI mean?
column2: Trading while aware of it.

column1: Rule 10b5-1: what is the affirmative defense?
column2: A binding contract, trading instruction, or written plan adopted before becoming aware.

column1: Rule 10b5-2: name the 3 situations that create a duty of trust or confidence.
column2: Agreement to keep confidential; history of sharing confidences; info from a spouse, parent, child, or sibling.

column1: Is info "public" if a limited group of outsiders knows it?
column2: No.

column1: § 16(b): who is covered and for what period?
column2: Officers, directors, >10% holders; profits within 6 months.

column1: Texas Gulf Sulphur: what must insiders with MNPI do?
column2: Disclose or abstain.

column1: TGS: when may insiders trade after an announcement?
column2: Only after the news is effectively disseminated (not minutes later).

column1: TGS: when is a company press release "in connection with" trading?
column2: When investors would rely on it.

column1: Chiarella: does possessing MNPI alone create a duty to disclose?
column2: No. The duty comes from a relationship of trust.

column1: Chiarella: why was the printer's conviction reversed?
column2: He owed target SHs no duty, and misappropriation wasn't put to the jury.

column1: Cady, Roberts: what are the 2 elements of a disclose-or-abstain duty?
column2: (i) Access to inside info meant for a corporate purpose; (ii) unfairness of trading on it.

column1: Dirks: when does a tippee inherit the duty to abstain?
column2: When the tipper breached by tipping for personal benefit and the tippee knew or should have known.

column1: Dirks: why was Dirks not liable?
column2: Secrist tipped to expose fraud, not for personal benefit.

column1: Name 4 things that count as a tipper's personal benefit.
column2: Money, reputation, currying favor, a gift.

column1: Which case allowed defendants to rebut fraud-on-the-market with no-price-impact evidence at class certification?
column2: Halliburton Co. v. Erica P. John Fund.

column1: Which case denied class certification because a broker's lies were told privately to clients?
column2: West v. Prudential Securities.

column1: Which case held an analyst not liable because his tipper sought to expose fraud, not to benefit?
column2: Dirks v. SEC.

column1: Which case held a financial printer who decoded takeover targets owed no duty to their SHs?
column2: Chiarella v. United States.

column1: Which case required insiders to disclose or abstain after a secret ore strike?
column2: SEC v. Texas Gulf Sulphur.

column1: Which case held an LLC member with management roles held no "security"?
column2: Robinson v. Glynn.

column1: What is the default voting rule for stock?
column2: One share, one vote.

column1: MBCA § 6.01(b): what 2 rights must exist in some class?
column2: Unlimited voting and the residual claim on assets (can be the same class).

column1: Name 3 ways to separate voting from economic rights.
column2: Any 3: dual-class stock; nonvoting stock; voting trusts; vote-pooling agreements; irrevocable proxies.

column1: When is a proxy irrevocable?
column2: When coupled with an interest (e.g., employment or a loan); default is revocable.

column1: MBCA § 7.02 vs. DGCL § 211(d): who can call a special meeting?
column2: MBCA: board or 10% holders. DE: board or those authorized in charter/bylaws.

column1: DGCL § 228: can SHs act without a meeting?
column2: Yes, by written consent of holders with the votes needed, unless the charter opts out.

column1: DGCL § 228(e): what must be given after action by written consent?
column2: Prompt notice to non-consenting SHs.

column1: Stroh v. Blackhawk: can stock carry voting rights with no economic rights?
column2: Yes.

column1: Stroh: why was the voting-only Class B valid?
column2: The statute lists control OR profits OR assets in the disjunctive.

column1: Espinoza v. Zuckerberg: can a controller ratify informally (e.g., by affidavit)?
column2: No. Only by a vote at a meeting or § 228 written consent.

column1: Espinoza: what standard applied to directors setting their own pay?
column2: Entire fairness.

column1: Federal vs. state law in SH voting?
column2: Federal: procedure and disclosure. State: substance (who votes, when, on what).

column1: Exchange Act § 14(a): what does it regulate?
column2: Proxy solicitations for § 12-registered securities.

column1: Name the 3 most common § 14(a) violations.
column2: Soliciting before a proxy statement; using unfiled materials; false or misleading solicitations.

column1: Rule 14a-2(b)(2): how many people can be solicited without the proxy rules?
column2: 10 or fewer.

column1: Rosenfeld: when may incumbents spend corporate funds on a proxy fight?
column2: In a policy contest (not a purely personal power fight), on reasonable and proper expenses.

column1: Rosenfeld: when are incumbents reimbursed?
column2: Win or lose.

column1: Rosenfeld: when are insurgents reimbursed?
column2: Only if they win and SHs ratify.

column1: DGCL § 113: what may bylaws provide?
column2: Reimbursement of a SH's proxy expenses in director elections, subject to conditions.

column1: J.I. Case v. Borak: is there a private right of action under § 14(a)?
column2: Yes, implied, both direct and derivative.

column1: Borak: why did the Court imply a private action?
column2: The SEC can't check thousands of proxies; private suits supplement enforcement.

column1: Which case held informal assent by a controller can't ratify directors' pay?
column2: Espinoza v. Zuckerberg.

column1: Which case upheld voting-only Class B stock with no dividend or liquidation rights?
column2: Stroh v. Blackhawk Holding Corp.

column1: Which case allowed reimbursement of proxy-fight costs in a policy contest?
column2: Rosenfeld v. Fairchild Engine & Airplane.

column1: Which case implied a private right of action under § 14(a)?
column2: J.I. Case Co. v. Borak.

column1: Rule 14a-8(b): what are the 3 ownership thresholds?
column2: $2,000 for 3 years; $15,000 for 2 years; $25,000 for 1 year.

column1: Rule 14a-8: how many proposals per proponent per meeting?
column2: One.

column1: Rule 14a-8(d): what is the word limit?
column2: 500 words.

column1: Rule 14a-8: what is the submission deadline?
column2: At least 120 days before the anniversary of last year's proxy release.

column1: Rule 14a-8(f): how long does each side get for a fixable defect?
column2: Company notifies within 14 days; proponent has 14 days to cure.

column1: Rule 14a-8(h): what if the proponent skips the meeting without good cause?
column2: Company may exclude their proposals for 2 years.

column1: Why are most SH proposals precatory?
column2: A binding proposal can be improper under state law ((i)(1)).

column1: What does an SEC no-action letter do?
column2: Says staff won't object if the company omits the proposal.

column1: Rule 14a-8(i)(5): when is a proposal excludable as irrelevant?
column2: <5% of assets, net earnings, and gross sales, and not otherwise significantly related to the business.

column1: Rule 14a-8(i)(7) excludes proposals about...
column2: Ordinary business operations.

column1: Rule 14a-8(i)(8) excludes proposals about...
column2: Director elections.

column1: Rule 14a-8(i)(12): what support thresholds allow excluding resubmissions?
column2: Under 5% (once), 15% (twice), 25% (three+ times) within 5 years.

column1: Lovenheim: can "otherwise significantly related" be non-economic?
column2: Yes. Ethical or social significance is enough.

column1: Which case required a company to include a foie gras proposal despite its tiny revenue?
column2: Lovenheim v. Iroquois Brands.

column1: Trinity v. Wal-Mart: when is an ordinary-business proposal NOT excludable?
column2: When it raises a significant policy issue that transcends day-to-day business.

column1: Trinity: why was the gun-sales proposal excludable?
column2: Product selection is core to a retailer's business, so the policy issue didn't transcend it.

column1: Trinity: matters handled without the board are generally...
column2: Excludable as ordinary business.

column1: AFSCME v. AIG: is a proxy-access procedure proposal excludable under the election exclusion?
column2: No. Only proposals about a particular election are.

column1: Rule 14a-7: what 2 options does the company have when a SH wants to solicit others?
column2: Mail the SH's materials (at SH's cost) or hand over the SH list.

column1: DGCL § 220(c): what 3 things must a SH show?
column2: SH status; compliance with form and manner; proper purpose.

column1: § 220: what makes a purpose "proper"?
column2: It is reasonably related to the person's interest as a stockholder.

column1: Name 4 accepted § 220 purposes.
column2: Any 4: valuing shares; evaluating an offer; director independence; testing disclosures; investigating waste or mismanagement.

column1: Is disagreeing with a business decision a proper § 220 purpose?
column2: No.

column1: § 220: what must a SH show to investigate wrongdoing?
column2: A credible basis, by a preponderance of the evidence.

column1: § 220: what scope of records does a SH get?
column2: Only those necessary and essential to the purpose.

column1: AmerisourceBergen: must the SH say how it will use the records?
column2: No, as long as it shows a credible basis.

column1: AmerisourceBergen: what is the exception?
column2: If litigation is the only stated use and an insurmountable procedural bar exists, the SH must state its plan.

column1: Crane v. Anaconda: may a tender offeror get the SH list?
column2: Yes, to communicate directly about its offer, unless the purpose harms the corporation.

column1: Crane: was the company's offer to mail Crane's materials enough?
column2: No. The SH chooses how to communicate.

column1: Pillsbury v. Honeywell: why was the purpose improper?
column2: It was purely political (opposing the war), not economic.

column1: Pillsbury: what kind of SH could have had a proper purpose?
column2: A bona fide investor worried about munitions' economic effects.

column1: Which case refused SH-list inspection to a SH who bought in to oppose munitions production?
column2: State ex rel. Pillsbury v. Honeywell.

column1: Which case held a tender offeror could get the target's SH list to answer management directly?
column2: Crane Co. v. Anaconda Co.

column1: Which case allowed excluding a gun-sales proposal as ordinary business?
column2: Trinity Wall Street v. Wal-Mart Stores.

column1: Which case held proxy-access procedure proposals aren't excludable under the election exclusion?
column2: AFSCME v. AIG.

column1: Which case held a SH need not say it plans to sue to inspect records about wrongdoing?
column2: AmerisourceBergen v. Lebanon County Employees' Retirement Fund.

column1: In re Match Group: does MFW apply beyond freeze-out mergers?
column2: Yes, to any controller transaction where the controller gets a non-ratable benefit.

column1: In re Match Group: how many special committee members must be independent?
column2: All of them, not just a majority.

column1: In re Match Group: what are the 2 parts of entire fairness?
column2: Fair dealing and fair price, considered together.

column1: Zahn v. Transamerica: what duty does a controlling SH acting through the board owe the minority?
column2: The same fiduciary duty as directors.

column1: Zahn: what was the breach?
column2: Redeeming Class A stock before liquidation so the controller's Class B captured the value.

column1: Which NY case gives an SLC's decision full BJR deference after checking its independence and procedures?
column2: Auerbach v. Bennett.

column1: Which case applied MFW to a non-freeze-out controller deal and required every committee member be independent?
column2: In re Match Group Derivative Litigation.

column1: Which case held a controller breached by redeeming Class A stock before liquidation?
column2: Zahn v. Transamerica.
